name: Sugar-free gum

lead: Sugar-free gum is chewing gum sweetened with sugar alcohols such as xylitol, sorbitol or maltitol. People chew it to freshen breath for a while and keep the mouth moist.

Chewing stimulates saliva, which clears food debris and buffers plaque acids, and dental researchers describe saliva as protective for teeth. Clinical trials of sugar-free gum have focused on cavities, including gums with added calcium-phosphate complexes for enamel remineralisation. Wikipedia notes that evidence for gum as a halitosis treatment is not supported by strong data.

paras: People chew a piece after meals or before social situations, in place of mints or sugary gum. The breath effect lasts while chewing and a short time after.
Large amounts of sorbitol or mannitol can cause gas or diarrhoea. Swallowed gum is a concern for young children.

angle.text: Sugar-free gum freshens breath for a while and boosts saliva, which dental researchers describe as protective for teeth. The dental trials concern cavities rather than appearance.

lead: Sugar-free chewing gum is gum sweetened with sugar alcohols such as xylitol, sorbitol, maltitol or isomalt, often with small amounts of intense sweeteners such as aspartame or sucralose.[1] In oral-care and appearance discussions it is used to freshen breath for a short time, keep the mouth moist and stimulate saliva, which dental researchers describe as protective for teeth and gums.[2][3] Cleaner, healthier-looking teeth and fresher breath are the appearance payoff people point to.

Clinical research on sugar-free gum has concentrated on tooth decay and plaque. Systematic reviews report that sugar-free gum reduced caries increment and plaque quantity compared with non-chewing controls,[4][5] and trials have tested gums containing added calcium-phosphate complexes for enamel remineralisation.[6][7] Wikipedia notes that evidence for gum as a halitosis treatment is not supported by strong data.[8]

Gum is also a long-standing everyday habit with a history reaching back to ancient resins and chicle, and it is a common companion to jaw-focused routines in appearance communities, though hard-chewing gum for jaw development is covered under its own entry.[1]
infobox: Xylitol, sorbitol, maltitol, isomalt, aspartame, sucralose[1]

paras: Sugar alcohols typically make up roughly 40 to 50 percent of a sugar-free gum formula, and their cooling sensation on dissolving is part of the gum's appeal.[1] Some products add fluoride or calcium compounds intended to support enamel, and some contain casein phosphopeptide-amorphous calcium phosphate (CPP-ACP, sold as Recaldent).[1][7]

Xylitol is the best-known sweetener in this category. It was isolated from beech wood chips by Emil Fischer and Rudolf Stahel in 1890, and interest in sugar substitutes grew with sugar rationing in World War II.[9] Xylitol provides about 2.4 kilocalories per gram against 4.0 for sucrose, and the US FDA considers it safe as a food additive.[9] Sorbitol is reported to protect teeth about a third as well as xylitol.[1]

Gum-like chewables date to the Neolithic: a roughly 5,000-year-old piece of birch bark tar with tooth imprints was found in Kierikki, Finland. The Maya and Aztecs chewed chicle, ancient Greeks chewed mastic resin, and North American peoples chewed spruce sap.[1] John B. Curtis sold the first commercial gum, The State of Maine Pure Spruce Gum, in 1848; paraffin gum overtook it around 1850.[1] An Ohio dentist, William F. Semple, patented a non-sweet gum in 1869 meant to clean teeth and strengthen the jaw, and Thomas Adams marketed chicle gum in 1871 after receiving the material from Antonio Lopez de Santa Anna.[1]

Brands such as Black Jack (1884), Chiclets (1899) and Wrigley's followed, American soldiers spread the habit worldwide in World War II, and by the 1960s synthetic rubber had replaced chicle in gum bases.[1] Sugar-free versions grew out of interest in sugar substitutes and caries prevention, reviewed in the dental literature from the late 1990s.[10] Chewing gum has since been endorsed as a caries-preventive agent by the FDI World Dental Federation, the American Dental Association and the European Food Safety Authority, according to a 2023 review.[11]

Chewing increases salivary flow. Saliva dilutes and clears food debris, buffers plaque acids and supplies minerals to enamel, and reviews in the Journal of the American Dental Association describe these as protective functions.[2][3] Because stimulated saliva is also swallowed more often, chewing gum has been tested for clearing acid in reflux; a randomized study of 31 people with reflux symptoms examined its effect on clearance from the lower esophagus after a refluxogenic meal.[12]

Studies of sugar alcohols have also examined whether xylitol and sorbitol have direct caries-preventive effects, in addition to the saliva effect.[13] Reviews describe xylitol as suppressing Streptococcus mutans, a bacterium associated with decay.[9][14]

A review of seven clinical trials assessed chewing gum's effect on caries incidence and on mechanisms such as plaque acid neutralisation.[3] A 2020 systematic review and meta-analysis of twelve studies found that sugar-free gum reduced caries increment with a preventive fraction of 28 percent, rising to 33 percent when only the eight xylitol-gum trials were counted; the authors described the evidence as tentative, with considerable variability and trials of moderate quality, and recorded no adverse effects.[4]

A 2022 meta-analysis of eight articles reported that sugar-free gum significantly reduced plaque quantity compared with non-chewing controls.[5] A 2021 review of controlled trials examined Streptococcus mutans levels in gum chewers versus controls.[14] A randomized trial in school children aged 14 to 15 looked at plaque and gingivitis,[15] and a 2022 study examined chewing sugar-free gum and caries status in China.[16]

Randomised, double-blind in situ trials tested sugar-free gum with CPP-ACP for remineralising enamel lesions and increasing their acid resistance,[6][7] and a bitewing radiography study examined its effect on approximal caries.[17] Other work looked at whether stimulating saliva reduces enamel erosion in in situ and ex vivo models.[18] A community-level study examined caries prevention from sugar-substituted gum.[19]

Outside oral health, a 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis compared sugar-free gum with analgesic drugs for pain from fixed orthodontic appliances,[20] and a randomized trial reported that chewing gum increased energy expenditure before and after controlled breakfasts.[21] These studies address dental and general health; no trial has tested gum as an appearance treatment itself.

Large amounts of sorbitol- or mannitol-containing products can cause gas or diarrhoea, and absorption patterns differ between healthy people and people with irritable bowel syndrome.[1][22] About half of ingested xylitol is absorbed, and much of the rest is fermented by gut bacteria; an EU Scientific Committee on Food report in 1985 warned that 50 grams a day can cause diarrhoea.[9]

Xylitol is toxic to dogs, in which it triggers insulin release that can cause life-threatening low blood sugar and, at higher doses, liver injury, so veterinary reviews advise keeping xylitol gum away from pets.[9][23] Wikipedia also lists swallowed-gum concerns in young children and research into micro- and nanoplastics released during chewing.[1]

Gum sales in the United States declined in the early 21st century and fell about 30 percent during COVID-19, with later recovery driven largely by higher prices; the average pack rose from $1.70 in 2018 to $2.71 in 2023.[1] A 2021 budget-impact analysis modelled the economic benefits of increased sugar-free gum use in China.[24]

Gum is mentioned in appearance communities as a low-cost way to keep breath fresh and mouth moist and as a companion to oral-care routines. Discussion of hard-chewing gum for jaw development is a separate topic covered under its own entry. In diet-oriented lifting forums such as T Nation, sugar-free gum is mentioned alongside sugar-alcohol and sweetener choices for low-sugar eating.[25]
